script.opening: (Tearful.) "The health visitor weighed Noah and said he's dropped down the lines on his chart, and now I'm beside myself. Am I starving my own baby? I'm breastfeeding and I thought it was going okay, but maybe I haven't got enough milk, maybe I'm doing it all wrong. I feel like such a failure. Is something seriously wrong with him? Please just tell me what I'm doing wrong."

facts.text: Born at term, 3.4 kg (about the 50th centile). The health visitor said he has dropped from the 50th to just below the 9th centile over the last two months. You can show the red book on camera.

Breastfed only. Feeds very often — every 1–2 hours, "little snacky feeds", often falls asleep on the breast after 5 minutes. Sometimes your nipples hurt with a "lipstick" shape after feeds. You have never seen a breastfeeding specialist. No bottles or solids yet.
Brings up a little milk after most feeds, not forceful, never green or bloody. Stools yellow, soft, two or three a day. Five or six wet nappies a day.
Smiling, cooing, holding his head up, rolling. No coughs or infections, no breathing problems, no sweating with feeds. On video he looks alert and smiley, slim but not unwell.
Normal pregnancy and birth. Newborn check normal. Immunisations up to date.

facts.topic: You — only if asked how you are
facts.text: You are 29, first baby. Exhausted, sleeping in 1–2 hour chunks, crying most days, feel "useless". Partner works long shifts. You enjoy cuddles with Noah but feel anxious all the time. No thoughts of harming yourself or Noah.
You are 5'3", your partner 5'8". Both were "small babies".

Tearful, expecting to be blamed. If the doctor asks clipped questions without acknowledging your feelings, get more upset: "So it IS my fault." If they reassure you that this is common, not your fault, and that they will work it out with you, calm down. Welcome practical help (feeding specialist, weight checks) and accept support for yourself if offered kindly.

ice.ideas: "I haven't got enough milk — I'm starving him."
ice.concerns: "Is something seriously wrong with him?" and that you are failing as a mum.
ice.expectations: "Tell me what I'm doing wrong." You want a plan and to be told he is going to be okay.

cues: "I feel like such a failure." — say in the opening.
"He falls asleep on the breast after five minutes." — say when describing feeds.
"I cry most days, to be honest." — say if asked how you are coping.

checkpoints.text: Approaches faltering growth with a STRUCTURED, NON-BLAMING assessment: careful feeding/dietary history, birth/medical/developmental history, examination, and accurate plotting (correct chart, prematurity, mid-parental size, regression to mean, measurement error) — rather than assuming maternal fault
Assesses FEEDING closely (breastfeeding attachment/positioning, frequency/volume, posseting/vomiting, stools, satisfaction) and observes/plans to observe a feed and involve feeding/lactation support

EXCLUDES organic red flags: significant/projectile vomiting, diarrhoea/malabsorption, recurrent infections, dysmorphism, developmental concerns, signs of illness — and considers safeguarding only where genuinely indicated; refers to paediatrics/dietetics if red flags or no improvement

Recognises that most faltering growth is NON-ORGANIC/feeding-related and plans practical support and MONITORING (regular weights with the health visitor, feeding plan, top-ups only as guided) rather than alarm or unnecessary investigation

Assesses and supports MATERNAL MENTAL HEALTH — screens for postnatal depression/anxiety, exhaustion and breastfeeding confidence — recognising this as central to the consultation and the baby’s feeding
RELIEVES THE GUILT explicitly: faltering growth is usually not her fault and she is not "starving" her baby; seeking help is good mothering — responding to the tears and self-blame first
Works in PARTNERSHIP and validates her efforts and distress, framing the plan as support not judgement, and engaging the health visitor as an ally

Safety-nets and follows up: feeding support and a monitoring plan with the health visitor, what would prompt paediatric/dietetic referral or concern (red flags, no weight improvement), maternal-mental-health support/follow-up, and a review — partnership and reassurance, not blame

worked.txt: "Stop — before anything else: you are NOT starving your baby, and you are not failing. Please hear that. Lots of babies cross the lines on the chart, and the great majority is to do with feeding getting established, not a mum doing anything wrong. The fact you’re this worried tells me what a good, attentive mum you are. Let’s work it out together, with no blame at all."

"Charts can be misleading on their own — babies don’t grow in straight lines, and one reading can wobble. So what I’d like to do is look at the whole picture properly: how feeding’s going, how Noah is in himself, examine him — I can’t do that properly on video, so I’d like to see you both in person at the surgery, ideally with a feed I can watch — and plot his weights carefully over time rather than panic at one drop."

"Tell me about the breastfeeding — how often, how long, does he seem satisfied, any sicking up, what are his nappies like? … It would really help to watch a feed, and I’d love to get you some proper feeding support — a few small tweaks to attachment can make a big difference, and that’s not a criticism, it’s just help."

"A few things I want to be sure about — is he vomiting forcefully, lots of diarrhoea, lots of infections, otherwise developing and alert? … Good. Those would make me look further; without them, this is most likely about supporting the feeding, and we’ll keep a close eye with regular weights."

"And can I ask how YOU are? You’re exhausted and in tears, and that matters to me too — looking after a baby on no sleep while worrying like this is so hard. How’s your mood been? … You don’t have to carry this alone; if things are low, we can help with that as well."

"So: feeding support, regular weight checks with your health visitor, examine Noah in person at the surgery today, and we look after you too. If he were to keep dropping, or any of those warning signs appeared, we’d involve the children’s team — but I don’t expect that. Come back and see me, and let’s do this as a team. You’re doing a good job."

f.learning: Faltering growth (a sustained fall across centile spaces / slower-than-expected weight gain) needs a STRUCTURED, NON-BLAMING assessment — careful feeding and medical/developmental history, examination, and accurate plotting (correct chart, prematurity, mid-parental size, regression to the mean, measurement error) — and most is NON-ORGANIC and feeding-related, not a sign the mother is "starving" her baby. Assess feeding closely (breastfeeding attachment/positioning, frequency, posseting, stools; observe a feed; involve lactation support), EXCLUDE organic red flags (significant vomiting, diarrhoea/malabsorption, recurrent infections, dysmorphism, developmental concerns) and consider safeguarding only where indicated, and manage with practical support and MONITORING (regular weights with the health visitor; paediatric/dietetic referral if red flags or no improvement). The examinable hidden agenda is the MOTHER: exhaustion, guilt, a sense of failing and possible postnatal depression with crumbling breastfeeding confidence — relieve the blame explicitly (it is usually not her fault; seeking help is good mothering), assess and support her mental health, and frame everything as partnership not judgement.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG75 — Faltering growth · UK-WHO growth charts (RCPCH) · NICE CG192 — Antenatal and postnatal mental health
knowledge.summary: Faltering growth needs a structured, non-blaming assessment: feeding history, an observed feed, examination and careful plotting over time. Most cases relate to feeding and settle with support. Look for red flags, and look after the mother.

points.t: NICE NG75 thresholds depend on birthweight centile: a fall across 1 or more centile spaces if birthweight was below the 9th centile, 2 or more if between the 9th and 91st, 3 or more if above the 91st, or current weight below the 2nd centile. Check Noah’s birthweight centile before labelling.

Use the UK-WHO chart, correct for prematurity, and read the trend across several weights. Measure length too. NICE NG75: weigh no more than weekly between 1 and 6 months — more frequent weighing adds noise and anxiety.

Frequency and length of feeds, attachment and positioning, signs of milk transfer, posseting or vomiting, stools and wet nappies. NICE NG75: observe a feed and involve trained infant-feeding support. Consider supplementation only after breastfeeding has been assessed and supported.

NICE NG75 refers when there are signs of an underlying disorder, primary care interventions have failed, linear growth is slow, there is rapid weight loss or severe undernutrition, or there is a safeguarding concern. Examples: forceful or bilious vomiting, chronic diarrhoea, recurrent infections, dysmorphism, developmental concerns.
Routine blood tests aren’t needed if feeding explains the picture. NICE NG75 suggests urine testing for UTI (per NICE NG224) and coeliac testing only once gluten is in the diet (NICE NG20).
NICE CG192: ask about depression and anxiety using the Whooley questions and GAD-2. Guilt, exhaustion and low mood affect feeding confidence and are part of this consultation.

dg.d: Responded to tears first; open question; let her explain the health visitor’s concern in her own words.
Exhaustion, support at home, breastfeeding confidence, and how the weight news affected her.
Face-to-face examination, length and weight plotted on UK-WHO chart, birthweight centile, observed feed; tests only if indicated.
Feeding-related (milk transfer, attachment) vs reflux, malabsorption, infection or other organic cause.
Screened forceful or bilious vomiting, stools, nappies, recurrent infections, development; maternal self-harm risk.
Explained probable feeding-related faltering growth without blame, pending examination and plotting.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Infant-feeding support, weekly weights at most, supplementation only after feeding assessment, referral criteria per NICE NG75.
Maternal mood screened with Whooley and GAD-2; follow-up and health visitor support for her.
Review this week, mood review in two weeks, specific red flags for Noah and crisis routes for her.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “I feel like a failure” and “am I starving him” and explored mood and guilt.
Idea of not enough milk; fear of serious illness and of failing; expectation to be told what she’s doing wrong.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — "Is something seriously wrong with him?" and that you are failing as a mum — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, I’m Dr Rahman. Can you hear and see me okay? And can I check Noah’s date of birth? … Thank you. I can see you’re upset — take your time and tell me what’s happened.
model.why: Video checks, then responds to visible distress before any agenda

model.text: The health visitor weighed him and said he’s dropped down the lines. Am I starving my own baby? Maybe I haven’t got enough milk. I feel like such a failure. Please just tell me what I’m doing wrong.

Before anything else: nothing you’ve said makes me think you’re starving Noah, and you are not a failure. Lots of babies cross lines on the chart, and it’s usually about feeding needing some support, not a parent doing something wrong. Let’s work it out together.
(Crying.) Sorry. I’ve just been so worried.
Please don’t apologise. I’d like to hear about his feeding, how he is generally, and how you are — then we’ll make a plan. Is that okay?
model.why: Sets a clear agenda that includes the mother

model.text: Tell me about a typical day of feeding.
He feeds a lot, but little and often. He brings some back after most feeds.
When he brings milk back, is it a small posset, or forceful vomiting that shoots out? And is it ever green?
Just small amounts dribbling out. Never green, never shooting.
That’s helpful. What are his nappies like — wet ones through the day, and his poos?
model.why: Hydration and stool screen for malabsorption

model.text: I think they’re normal. I’ve not noticed anything strange.
And in himself — alert, smiling, doing the things you’d expect? Any coughs, chest infections or illnesses?
He’s alert and smiley. No illnesses I can think of.
Good. Do you know roughly what centile he was born on, and was he born around his due date?
model.why: Birthweight centile and prematurity change how the drop is interpreted

model.text: I’d need to check his red book.

No problem — I’ll look at the red book and the health visitor’s plotting with you. Could you hold Noah up so I can see him? … He looks alert and comfortable on camera. I’ll still need to examine him properly in person.
model.why: Uses the video for observation but recognises its limits

model.text: Can I ask how you are? You said you feel like a failure. How has your mood been over the last few weeks?
Exhausted. I cry a lot. I thought breastfeeding was going okay, and now I don’t trust myself at all.

Thank you for telling me. Over the past month, have you often felt down or hopeless, or had little interest or pleasure in doing things? And have you felt nervous or on edge, or unable to stop worrying?
The worrying, yes, all the time. Down some days. I still want to do things with him.
Any thoughts of harming yourself, or that he’d be better off without you?
No. Never that. I just want to get it right for him.

From what you’ve told me, Noah is alert, has no worrying vomiting, normal nappies and no illnesses. That makes it very likely this is about feeding — possibly how well milk is getting through at each feed — rather than anything serious. And none of this means you’ve done anything wrong.
model.why: Shares a working analysis based on the red-flag screen

model.text: So it’s not something wrong with him?
Nothing so far points that way, but I want to examine him properly to be sure, and look carefully at the chart over time. One weight can wobble; the trend tells us more.

Here’s what I suggest. I see Noah in person this week to examine him and plot everything carefully. I ask an infant-feeding specialist to watch a feed with you — small changes to latch can make a big difference. Your health visitor weighs him once a week, not more. Does that sound manageable?
model.why: Structured plan: examination, observed feed, feeding support, measured monitoring

model.text: Yes. Should I be giving him formula?

Let’s get the feeding assessed first. If top-ups turn out to be needed, we’ll plan them with the feeding team so they support your breastfeeding rather than replace it — that’s your choice to make with us.
model.why: Shared decision on supplementation, in line with NICE NG75

model.text: Okay. That feels better than guessing.
And for you: I’d like to see you again in two weeks to see how your mood is. Your health visitor can support you in between. If things feel heavier, you can talk to someone sooner.
model.why: Maternal mental-health follow-up built into the plan

model.text: Contact us the same day if Noah vomits forcefully or brings up anything green, has far fewer wet nappies, becomes floppy or unusually sleepy, or you’re very worried. And if you ever have thoughts of harming yourself, please call us or NHS 111 straight away. When someone at home asks what the doctor said, what will you tell them?
model.why: Specific safety-net for both and teach-back

model.text: That I’m not starving him. The doctor will check him this week, someone will watch a feed, and I’ll come back about me.
That’s it. You’re clearly a caring, attentive mum — that’s why you noticed and why you’re here. We’ll do this together.
Thank you. I feel like I can breathe again.

social.t: Frequent feeds and broken nights wear parents down. Ask who helps at home and what support is available.
Weight concerns often lead to early stopping. Practical infant-feeding support protects breastfeeding if she wants to continue.

legal.t: Faltering growth is rarely neglect. NICE NG75 lists safeguarding concern as a referral trigger, but consider it only when there are genuine indicators; nothing in this history suggests it.

professional.t: Agree who weighs, how often and who reviews the chart. Shared records reduce conflicting advice to an anxious parent.
Observation on video helps, but examination and accurate measurement need a face-to-face appointment. Document why it is arranged.

community.t: Infant-feeding specialist or lactation service, local breastfeeding groups, the National Breastfeeding Helpline, and perinatal mental-health support via the GP or health visitor.

redFlags: Forceful or bilious vomiting, blood in stools, chronic diarrhoea
Recurrent infections, dysmorphism, developmental concerns, floppiness
Rapid weight loss or severe undernutrition; maternal thoughts of self-harm
psychosocial: Mother’s mood, sleep and support at home
Breastfeeding confidence and her own feeding goals
Relationship with the health visitor and the advice she has had
ice: Idea: “I haven’t got enough milk — I’m starving him.”
Concern: failing as a mother, or something seriously wrong with Noah
Expectation: to be told what she’s doing wrong

playbook.diagnosis: Frame it without blame: “From everything you’ve told me, this is most likely about feeding needing some support — how much milk gets through at each feed — not you doing anything wrong. I’ll examine him and look at the chart over time to be sure.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Growth charts are like a road with several lanes. Noah has drifted across a couple of lanes. That tells us to look, not that something is badly wrong — and most babies drift back once feeding is sorted.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked if you’re starving him. You’re not — and the fact you’re this worried shows how much you care.”
management.psychosocial: Build the plan around her: an observed feed with a specialist, weekly weights at most, and a follow-up for her mood as well as Noah’s weight.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face examination and careful plotting this week, including birthweight centile
Infant-feeding assessment with an observed feed; top-ups only after assessment
Weekly weights with the health visitor; paediatric referral if NICE NG75 triggers appear
safetyNet: Same-day contact for forceful or green vomiting, fewer wet nappies, floppiness or unusual sleepiness
Mood review in two weeks; call the surgery or NHS 111 urgently if thoughts of self-harm

pitfalls.intro: This station has two patients. Candidates who produce a perfect feeding plan while ignoring a tearful, exhausted mother fail the Relating domain; candidates who only comfort her miss the structured assessment.

items.fail: Starting the feeding history while she is still asking if she’s starving her baby.
items.why: “Did not respond to the patient’s emotions.” She won’t take in anything until the guilt is addressed.
items.fix: First sentence: “You are not starving him, and you’re not failing.” Then the history.

items.fail: Calling it faltering growth without checking birthweight centile or prematurity.
items.why: NICE NG75 thresholds depend on birthweight centile; a two-space drop may or may not meet the definition.
items.fix: Ask for the red book and look at the plotted trend with her.

items.why: “Management not in line with current guidance.” NICE NG75 puts breastfeeding assessment and support first.
items.fix: Arrange an observed feed and specialist feeding support, then decide on top-ups together.

items.fail: No red-flag screen, or ordering a battery of blood tests.
items.why: Either misses organic disease or over-investigates a likely feeding problem.
items.fix: Ask about vomiting, stools, infections and development; test only when indicated.

items.why: Postnatal depression and anxiety are common and affect feeding. Omitting it misses half the station.
items.fix: Use the Whooley and GAD-2 questions naturally, and ask directly about self-harm.

items.fail: Relying on the video view and not arranging an in-person examination.
items.why: “Examination not adequately planned.” Accurate weight, length and examination can’t be done on camera.
items.fix: “He looks well on screen, but I want to examine him properly this week.”

timeMap.d: She opens in tears asking if she’s starving him. Answer that first — no blame.
Feed pattern, posseting vs vomiting, nappies, illnesses, development, birthweight centile. Observe Noah on camera.
Whooley and GAD-2, self-harm question. Validate the exhaustion.
Likely feeding-related, not her fault; the trend matters more than one weight; examine in person.
Examination this week, observed feed, weekly weights, top-ups only after assessment, mood follow-up, red flags.

wordPics.fail: Launches into a feeding checklist while she cries; implies the milk supply is the problem or suggests switching to formula; no red-flag screen; no plan to examine; never asks how she is.
wordPics.pass: Reassures her it isn’t her fault; takes a feeding history and screens red flags; plans examination, plotting and feeding support; asks about her mood; arranges review.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: relieves guilt in the first minute; checks birthweight centile before labelling; uses NICE CG192 questions naturally; protects breastfeeding in the supplementation discussion; plans follow-up for mother and baby; she leaves feeling like a partner, not a suspect.

avoid.dont: “He’s not getting enough milk, so you’ll need to start formula top-ups.”
avoid.instead: “Let’s get the feeding looked at properly first — then decide together if top-ups would help.”
avoid.why: Jumping to formula confirms her fear of failing and bypasses NICE NG75.

avoid.dont: “Don’t worry, lots of babies drop centiles.”
avoid.instead: “You’re not failing — and I want to look at his whole picture carefully so we know exactly what’s going on.”
avoid.why: Blanket reassurance without assessment is unsafe and doesn’t address her guilt.

avoid.dont: “Let’s weigh him every couple of days to keep an eye.”
avoid.instead: “Once a week is enough — more often just adds worry without telling us more.”
avoid.why: Over-frequent weighing is noisy and fuels maternal anxiety; NICE NG75 limits it.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG75 — Faltering growth · UK-WHO growth charts (RCPCH) · NICE CG192 — Antenatal and postnatal mental health
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Faltering growth needs a structured, non-blaming assessment: feeding history, an observed feed, examination and careful plotting over time. Most cases relate to feeding and settle with support. Look for red flags, and look after the mother.

points.t: NICE NG75 thresholds depend on birthweight centile: a fall across 1 or more centile spaces if birthweight was below the 9th centile, 2 or more if between the 9th and 91st, 3 or more if above the 91st, or current weight below the 2nd centile. Check Noah’s birthweight centile before labelling.

Use the UK-WHO chart, correct for prematurity, and read the trend across several weights. Measure length too. NICE NG75: weigh no more than weekly between 1 and 6 months — more frequent weighing adds noise and anxiety.

Frequency and length of feeds, attachment and positioning, signs of milk transfer, posseting or vomiting, stools and wet nappies. NICE NG75: observe a feed and involve trained infant-feeding support. Consider supplementation only after breastfeeding has been assessed and supported.

NICE NG75 refers when there are signs of an underlying disorder, primary care interventions have failed, linear growth is slow, there is rapid weight loss or severe undernutrition, or there is a safeguarding concern. Examples: forceful or bilious vomiting, chronic diarrhoea, recurrent infections, dysmorphism, developmental concerns.
Routine blood tests aren’t needed if feeding explains the picture. NICE NG75 suggests urine testing for UTI (per NICE NG224) and coeliac testing only once gluten is in the diet (NICE NG20).
NICE CG192: ask about depression and anxiety using the Whooley questions and GAD-2. Guilt, exhaustion and low mood affect feeding confidence and are part of this consultation.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Responded to tears first; open question; let her explain the health visitor’s concern in her own words.
Exhaustion, support at home, breastfeeding confidence, and how the weight news affected her.
Picked up “I feel like a failure” and “am I starving him” and explored mood and guilt.
Idea of not enough milk; fear of serious illness and of failing; expectation to be told what she’s doing wrong.
Face-to-face examination, length and weight plotted on UK-WHO chart, birthweight centile, observed feed; tests only if indicated.
Feeding-related (milk transfer, attachment) vs reflux, malabsorption, infection or other organic cause.
Screened forceful or bilious vomiting, stools, nappies, recurrent infections, development; maternal self-harm risk.
Explained probable feeding-related faltering growth without blame, pending examination and plotting.
Infant-feeding support, weekly weights at most, supplementation only after feeding assessment, referral criteria per NICE NG75.
Maternal mood screened with Whooley and GAD-2; follow-up and health visitor support for her.
Review this week, mood review in two weeks, specific red flags for Noah and crisis routes for her.

social.t: Frequent feeds and broken nights wear parents down. Ask who helps at home and what support is available.
Weight concerns often lead to early stopping. Practical infant-feeding support protects breastfeeding if she wants to continue.

legal.t: Faltering growth is rarely neglect. NICE NG75 lists safeguarding concern as a referral trigger, but consider it only when there are genuine indicators; nothing in this history suggests it.

professional.t: Agree who weighs, how often and who reviews the chart. Shared records reduce conflicting advice to an anxious parent.
Observation on video helps, but examination and accurate measurement need a face-to-face appointment. Document why it is arranged.

community.t: Infant-feeding specialist or lactation service, local breastfeeding groups, the National Breastfeeding Helpline, and perinatal mental-health support via the GP or health visitor.

redFlags: Forceful or bilious vomiting, blood in stools, chronic diarrhoea
Recurrent infections, dysmorphism, developmental concerns, floppiness
Rapid weight loss or severe undernutrition; maternal thoughts of self-harm
psychosocial: Mother’s mood, sleep and support at home
Breastfeeding confidence and her own feeding goals
Relationship with the health visitor and the advice she has had
ice: Idea: “I haven’t got enough milk — I’m starving him.”
Concern: failing as a mother, or something seriously wrong with Noah
Expectation: to be told what she’s doing wrong

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Frame it without blame: “From everything you’ve told me, this is most likely about feeding needing some support — how much milk gets through at each feed — not you doing anything wrong. I’ll examine him and look at the chart over time to be sure.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Growth charts are like a road with several lanes. Noah has drifted across a couple of lanes. That tells us to look, not that something is badly wrong — and most babies drift back once feeding is sorted.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked if you’re starving him. You’re not — and the fact you’re this worried shows how much you care.”
management.psychosocial: Build the plan around her: an observed feed with a specialist, weekly weights at most, and a follow-up for her mood as well as Noah’s weight.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face examination and careful plotting this week, including birthweight centile
Infant-feeding assessment with an observed feed; top-ups only after assessment
Weekly weights with the health visitor; paediatric referral if NICE NG75 triggers appear
safetyNet: Same-day contact for forceful or green vomiting, fewer wet nappies, floppiness or unusual sleepiness
Mood review in two weeks; call the surgery or NHS 111 urgently if thoughts of self-harm

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station has two patients. Candidates who produce a perfect feeding plan while ignoring a tearful, exhausted mother fail the Relating domain; candidates who only comfort her miss the structured assessment.

items.fail: Starting the feeding history while she is still asking if she’s starving her baby.
items.why: “Did not respond to the patient’s emotions.” She won’t take in anything until the guilt is addressed.
items.fix: First sentence: “You are not starving him, and you’re not failing.” Then the history.

items.fail: Calling it faltering growth without checking birthweight centile or prematurity.
items.why: NICE NG75 thresholds depend on birthweight centile; a two-space drop may or may not meet the definition.
items.fix: Ask for the red book and look at the plotted trend with her.

items.why: “Management not in line with current guidance.” NICE NG75 puts breastfeeding assessment and support first.
items.fix: Arrange an observed feed and specialist feeding support, then decide on top-ups together.

items.fail: No red-flag screen, or ordering a battery of blood tests.
items.why: Either misses organic disease or over-investigates a likely feeding problem.
items.fix: Ask about vomiting, stools, infections and development; test only when indicated.

items.why: Postnatal depression and anxiety are common and affect feeding. Omitting it misses half the station.
items.fix: Use the Whooley and GAD-2 questions naturally, and ask directly about self-harm.

items.fail: Relying on the video view and not arranging an in-person examination.
items.why: “Examination not adequately planned.” Accurate weight, length and examination can’t be done on camera.
items.fix: “He looks well on screen, but I want to examine him properly this week.”
